To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
perceived and exerted control over pain have different effects on subsequent pain relief.

(i) exerted control on short and long pain stimuli is associated with increased activity in the anteromedial prefrontal cortex, dorsolateral pre‐ and postcentral gyrus and (ii) perceived control on short pain stimuli is associated increased activity in the orbitofron‐ tal and mediofrontal regions, and (iii) the neural correlates of exerted control on long pain stimuli are associated with increased activity of the anterolaterally prefrontal regions.
the sense of control (but no execution) and execution of control (but not sense) on pain elicit dissociable neural activity in the prefrontal cortex during pain relief.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of perceived vs. exert control over pain relief.
the neural mechanisms underlying pain control and the effects of perceived vs. exert control.
the effects of perceived and exert control over pain and its impact on subsequent pain relief in experimental pain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the neural correlates of the sense of control and the exertion of control differ and are related to different aspects of pain relief.

the sense of control and the execution of control on pain have different neural correlates and that the execution of pain control is more effective in attenuating pain perception than the sense of pain control.

the sense of control over pain is associated with a more pronounced activation of the medial orbitofrontal cortex, while exerted control over pain is more pronouncedly associated with activation of the anterolaterofrontal cortex.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
perceived and exerted control over pain are two distinct factors which affect subsequent pain relief by different mechanisms and neural pathways.
the neural correlates for pain relief are different depending on whether control over pain is perceived or exerted.
the neural correlates of perceived and exert ed pain control are dissociable.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the perceived and exerted control on painful stimulation have different neural signatures and that the exerted control is more effective in attenuating pain.
the neural mechanisms involved in the perception of pain control differ from the execution of pain control.
pain relief following exerted and perceived control is associated with different patterns of neural activity in the prefrontal and posterior cortex.
